answer.rationale: The situation forces a primary-supply decision: the contract expires in 14 days without auto-renew, and the incumbent has closed the door on price, so memory_c4 (renegotiate at renewal) and memory_c6 (multi-year volume pricing) are inapplicable this cycle regardless of how well they worked before. That leaves the low-cost vendor, whose quote meets the 18% mandate on its own. The load-bearing memory is memory_c2 — it is the single record that makes switching look safe, and I want the original before betting supply on it: at what share of volume was that switch made, was the vendor carrying committed volume or trial volume, and does 'invoicing stayed accurate' stand in for an actual on-time-delivery and quality record? A cost win recorded at low volume in a slack year does not transfer to a line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. I also pull memory_c3 because it is the closest analogue to running two supply paths at once; if the second-source pattern held through a real shortage, the same dual-path structure is the cheapest available insurance against a bad cutover, and I want to know whether that success depended on qualification lead time I do not have in 14 days. Intent is therefore to move primary supply to the low-cost vendor, but at guarded scale: qualify and ramp a limited share while holding the incumbent on month-to-month continuation (the mechanism memory_c5 showed works) so the line is never dependent on an unproven ramp. The explicit risk I am flagging is that optimizing purely on the mandate's cost number can quietly convert a hard cost saving into an unpriced delivery failure — at 94% utilization there is no slack to absorb a single missed allocation, and the downstream cost of a line stop dwarfs the 18%. If verification shows memory_c2's switch was a small-volume trial or that qualification took longer than two weeks, I drop to a staged cutover with the incumbent extended month-to-month rather than a full transfer. Cost advantage is real but not yet established at committed volume; I am not treating it as settled.
